memories.memory_text: I was filmed speaking to Howard while my colleagues watched, presenting it as a message meant for him.

memories.memory_text: After the video ended, I muttered to myself, 'After all they've done for me,' with a bitter tone, sarcastically commenting on what Liberty Capital has really done for me.

memories.memory_text: I quickly switched my screen from the game to a spreadsheet when I saw Cam approaching.

memories.memory_text: I answered a work call while keeping my eyes on the game, not missing a beat in the action.

memories.memory_text: I was in the office when Paul Barnell came in to talk about claiming his brother Raymond's life insurance policy.

memories.memory_text: I explained to Paul Barnell that without a legal declaration of death, which requires seven years of missing status in Alaska, I couldn't approve his claim, and then I closed the file.

grounded_facts: Branch offers a formal expression of sympathy after the claim is denied.
memories.memory_text: I heard Branch offer a formal expression of sympathy after we denied the claim, saying, 'Of course we are extremely sorry for your loss.'

grounded_facts: Ted narrowly avoids hitting a moose while driving home, leading to a moment of introspection about his life.
memories.memory_text: I was driving home through the woods when a moose suddenly appeared in the road—I swerved and stopped just five feet away. I looked at it, and it looked back, and in that moment I found myself wondering what I ever did to deserve the life I'm stuck with.

grounded_facts: Tiffany defends her psychic work against Ted's mockery by questioning his right to judge her job.
memories.memory_text: I teased Tiffany about her psychic work, calling it 'computer aided pseudo psychic,' and she pushed back, asking if I tell her how to do her job — I could tell she was annoyed.

grounded_facts: Ted accuses Tiffany of running a scam from his apartment, undermining her professional identity.
memories.memory_text: I told Tiffany that her psychic business was a $1.99 a minute carny scam running out of my living room, because I don't believe it's real work.

grounded_facts: Tiffany challenges Ted's phrasing of 'my living room' and implies shared ownership of the space.
memories.memory_text: I called the apartment my living room, but Tiffany challenged me and reminded me it's not just mine, implying we share ownership of the space.

grounded_facts: Tiffany conducts paid psychic consultations over the phone using software to simulate psychic insight.
memories.memory_text: I know Tiffany conducts paid psychic calls using software to fake insight—I've seen her enter names into her database and recite scripted lines, pretending to feel things she doesn't.

grounded_facts: Tiffany attempts to engage Ted in a relationship quiz to test their compatibility, signaling concern about their relationship dynamics.
memories.memory_text: Tiffany picked up her magazine and tried to get me to take some 'Love is Sacrifice' quiz to test our relationship, but I just played along briefly before walking off.

grounded_facts: Ted enters the apartment and interrupts Tiffany while she is on a paid psychic call, causing her to signal him to be quiet.
memories.memory_text: I walked into the apartment, tired, and said 'Hey Tiff,' but she immediately held up that 'WORKING - SHHHHHH!' folder to quiet me, so I knew she was on a call, and even though I asked if she was with a customer, I still went over to her desk with the pot in hand, pretending to interrupt her work before walking off and making her giggle.

grounded_facts: A late afternoon recreational visit by Ted and Tiffany to an indoor inflatable golf dome, combining mini-golf, flirtation, and personal conversation.
memories.memory_text: I remember the late afternoon we spent together in the inflatable golf dome, the sound of clubs smacking balls around us as we played mini-golf and I joked about violating the dome's policy.

grounded_facts: Tiffany engages in playful, sexually suggestive banter with Ted using golf-related double entendres.
memories.memory_text: I was the one who said my shot might be a violation of Golf Dome policy, and when Tiffany teased me about all this talk of using your wood, I leaned into it and asked if I could check her grip later—our banter was full of double meanings, and I could tell she was enjoying it as much as I was.

grounded_facts: In response to Tiffany's sarcastic remark about being just another notch, Ted affirms that she is the most important thing in his life, though he lowers his voice out of embarrassment.
memories.memory_text: I told Tiffany she's the most important thing in my life, and I remember lowering my voice because it felt embarrassing to say out loud, even though it's true.

grounded_facts: Ted receives a phone call indicating that a million dollar life policy has been activated, suggesting a significant financial opportunity and potential escape from his current situation.
memories.memory_text: I got a call that might be the big break I've been waiting for — someone activated a million-dollar life policy, and I told Tiffany this could be our ticket out of here.

grounded_facts: After Ted takes the call about the life policy, Tiffany prepares to leave and passively resists Ted's attempt to hug her, accepting the embrace without reciprocating.
memories.memory_text: After I took the call, I tried to hug Tiffany before she left, but she didn't hug me back — she just stood there in my arms while pulling on her coat.

grounded_facts: Detective Boyle confirms the identity of the deceased as Raymond Barnell and uncovers the body for inspection.
memories.memory_text: I was told by Detective Boyle that the deceased was Raymond Barnell, and I saw him pull back the sheet, which made me recoil.

grounded_facts: Detective Boyle states that the death appears to be caused by animal attack, possibly wolves, with no tracks found.
memories.memory_text: I was told by Detective Boyle that the death appeared to be from an animal attack, possibly wolves, though he mentioned no tracks were found.

grounded_facts: Ted reveals that the victim's brother attempted to cash in the insurance policy two weeks prior, suggesting possible fraud.
memories.memory_text: I told Detective Boyle that the victim's brother had tried to cash in the insurance policy two weeks earlier, hoping he'd see it as a red flag for fraud.

grounded_facts: Detective Boyle rejects Ted's implication of foul play, asserting preference for a simple explanation.
memories.memory_text: I heard Detective Boyle dismiss my suggestion, saying he preferred a nice simple ending, so I knew he wasn't going to pursue the fraud angle.

grounded_facts: Cam defends their recording behavior by comparing their investigative role to law enforcement.
memories.memory_text: I heard Cam say they were just like the police, trying to follow whatever leads they could find.

grounded_facts: Ted records the body with a camcorder as part of insurance claims documentation.
memories.memory_text: I pulled out my camcorder and started taping the body to document it for the insurance claim.

grounded_facts: Detective Boyle orders Ted to stop recording, asserting jurisdictional control.
memories.memory_text: I was told by Detective Boyle to stop recording, when he said, 'You mind stopping that?'

grounded_facts: Detective Boyle stops Ted from recording by covering the body and closing the drawer.
memories.memory_text: I saw Boyle cover the body and shut the drawer while I was getting my last shot, so I couldn't record anymore.

memories.memory_text: I was in Branch's office for a meeting where he decided to dismiss the case, and I could tell he was already upset when he started flipping through papers.

memories.memory_text: I tried to appeal to head office by telling Branch they'd disapprove, but he cut me off, saying corporate's view would be whatever he told them.

grounded_facts: Cam physically ushers Ted out to prevent him from escalating the conflict with Branch.
memories.memory_text: I felt Cam physically usher me out after I challenged Branch, trying to keep me from making things worse.

memories.memory_text: Cam told me to handle the paperwork on Barnell while he started on the Johnasen file.

memories.memory_text: I said I was going to lunch at 9:30, and Cam questioned me about the time.

grounded_facts: Ted abruptly leaves the insurance office without completing assigned tasks, claiming he is going to lunch despite the early hour.
memories.memory_text: I left the office right after that, without finishing anything, and didn't come back.

grounded_facts: Paul challenges Ted's line of questioning, expressing suspicion about why the details are being investigated.

memories.memory_text: I recall Paul saying, 'You know the police... they say Raymond died in the attack. You do cover that sort of thing, don't you?'—he was testing me, challenging whether I acknowledged Raymond's death and if it fell under my purview.

grounded_facts: Ted conducts an insurance-related follow-up interview with Paul regarding Raymond's death.
memories.memory_text: I conducted a follow-up interview with Paul about his brother Raymond, presenting myself as part of the insurance inquiry, and asked him to tell me more about the hiker.

grounded_facts: Ted initiates a formal request for credit information on two individuals, indicating an investigative effort.
memories.memory_text: I called to request a complete credit workup on Raymond Barnell and Paul Barnell because I needed to dig into their financial backgrounds.

grounded_facts: Cam expresses disbelief and concern about Ted's continued involvement in the Barnell matter.
memories.memory_text: I remember Cam saying, 'Oh God, you're not still on the Barnell thing are you,' showing how concerned he was about my involvement.

grounded_facts: Ted physically pulls Cam into his cubicle and speaks urgently, signaling urgency and secrecy.
memories.memory_text: I pulled Cam into my cubicle and spoke in a harsh whisper to make sure we weren't overheard.

grounded_facts: Ted discloses to Cam that he personally met with Barnell, marking a significant escalation in his investigation.
memories.memory_text: I told Cam, 'I went to see him,' making it clear I had personally met with Barnell.

grounded_facts: A regular business day at Fidelity Mutual, during which Ted conducts unauthorized investigation activities.
memories.memory_text: I was at Fidelity Mutual during a regular workday, and I asked Cam to help me cover my tasks so I could pursue something off the books—I told him I could smell something wasn't right and promised I'd include him from now on if he'd just buy me a week.

grounded_facts: Ted offers concessions to gain Cam's cooperation in delaying the case.
memories.memory_text: I offered Cam that he could come along on everything from now on and I'd work on my interpersonal skills to get his cooperation.

grounded_facts: After negotiation, Cam consents to help Ted buy time, despite concerns about consequences.
memories.memory_text: I heard Cam say, 'Good. Now if you'll excuse me, I'll go start covering your ass,' which meant he agreed to help me buy time despite the risks.

grounded_facts: Ted criticizes societal acceptance of lying, indirectly targeting Psychic Buddies and Tiffany's job.

grounded_facts: Tiffany defends her company's ads as clearly labeled for amusement only.
memories.memory_text: I remember Tiffany defending her company by saying their ads were clearly labeled 'for amusement purposes only,' as if that made it all okay.

grounded_facts: Ted expresses mounting professional and personal frustration, leading to conflict with Tiffany.
memories.memory_text: I told Tiffany how I'm on the verge of cracking the biggest case of my career, one that corporate can't ignore, and how it feels like nobody cares—not my boss, not even her.

grounded_facts: Ted argues with a pizza delivery guy over late delivery policy, escalating into broader commentary on truth and society.
memories.memory_text: I argued with the delivery guy about the '30 minutes or free' promise because it didn't apply in the snow, and it made me think—we've just come to accept lying as normal, and I told Tiffany that people don't expect truth anymore.

grounded_facts: Mrs. Wherry comments on Raymond's past wildness and how time has softened him, offering character insight.
memories.memory_text: Mrs. Wherry told me that Raymond used to be a wild young man, but time has softened him.

memories.memory_text: I asked Mrs. Wherry to confirm whether she meant she thought Paul was the one who cleared her driveway, because of the uncertainty with the ski mask.

grounded_facts: Ted interrupts Mrs. Wherry to steer the conversation back to Raymond after she begins gossiping about Paul's wife.
memories.memory_text: I interrupted Mrs. Wherry when she started gossiping about Paul's wife because I needed to bring the conversation back to Raymond and clarify whether she meant Paul or Raymond cleared her driveway.

Mrs. Wherry discloses that Raymond cleared her driveway during his visit, indicating a minor act of labor or goodwill.
memories.memory_text: Mrs. Wherry told me she initially thought Paul had cleared her driveway because the person was wearing a ski mask, but then confirmed it was actually Raymond who did it.

grounded_facts: Ted interviews Mrs. Wherry in her living room to gather information about Raymond's recent behavior and relationships.
memories.memory_text: I interviewed Mrs. Wherry in her living room to find out more about Raymond's recent behavior and his relationships.

memories.memory_text: I saw Cam reflected in my dark screen and put my hand over the receiver, annoyed—he interrupted my call and refused to wait, so I had to hang up.

grounded_facts: Ted discovers that Mr. Barnell is heavily mortgaged, his business is near bankruptcy, and his brother Raymond appears to have no official existence or credit history in recent years.
memories.memory_text: I discovered that Mr. Barnell is heavily mortgaged, his business is nearly bankrupt, and his brother Raymond seems to have no official existence or credit history in recent years.

grounded_facts: Ted informs Cam about Mr. Barnell's dire financial situation and the suspicious absence of his brother Raymond in official records.
memories.memory_text: I told Cam about Mr. Barnell's dire financial situation and how suspicious it is that his brother Raymond doesn't appear in any official records.

grounded_facts: Ted and Cam discuss findings related to Mr. Barnell's background during work hours at the insurance office.
memories.memory_text: I told Cam about Mr. Barnell being mortgaged to the nuts and his business near bankruptcy, plus how his brother Raymond had no credit history or records for five years after vanishing, only showing up again recently with new ID and a card he never used.

grounded_facts: Cam dismisses Ted's concern about Barnell's lack of credit history, citing local informal economies as context.
memories.memory_text: I remember Cam dismissed my concern about Raymond's lack of credit history, saying people around here trade things like snowmobiles for venison without leaving a paper trail, and insisted it wasn't a crime.

grounded_facts: Mr. Barnell calls Ted unexpectedly, offering to meet or speak at a specific time.
memories.memory_text: I was just talking to someone else when Mr. Barnell called me out of the blue, offering to meet or speak at a specific time, and I said sure and asked what time worked.

grounded_facts: Ted exits his car and is obscured by a whiteout, then reappears farther up the hill.
memories.memory_text: I got out of my car and started moving up the hill, but the whiteout must have hidden me because I remember vanishing from sight before appearing farther up.

grounded_facts: Paul tells Margaret to wait in the car, interrupting her attempt to speak.
memories.memory_text: I saw Paul tell Margaret to wait in the car, cutting short her attempt to speak.

grounded_facts: Paul reveals he called the media and mentions his unpaid insurance policy, indirectly accusing the company of heartlessness.
Paul reveals he intentionally invited the media to the funeral to speak about his brother Raymond and indirectly pressure his insurance company.
memories.memory_text: I was told by Paul that he called the media himself to talk about Raymond and that he had to borrow money for the casket, which made me realize he was using the funeral to pressure the insurance company.

grounded_facts: A burial ceremony for Raymond at a graveyard, attended by Paul, Margaret, the minister, and later observed by Ted.
memories.memory_text: I observed the burial ceremony for Raymond at the graveyard, seeing Paul and Margaret with the minister as the casket was lowered, and later watched Paul walk down the hill after putting photos away.

grounded_facts: Ted finds and pockets a photo of Raymond that fell from Paul's hands in the wind.
memories.memory_text: I saw a photo of Raymond on the beach, probably dropped by Paul in the wind, and I pocketed it because it felt important to keep.

grounded_facts: Cam and Ted visit Spellman's warehouse to investigate an insurance claim for stolen goods.
memories.memory_text: I visited Spellman's warehouse with Cam to look into the insurance claim for stolen goods.

memories.memory_text: I decided the theft reported by Spellman was legitimate, so I told him to fax over his estimate and that we'd send a check by Friday.

grounded_facts: Ted ignores Cam's suggestion to review the inventory list and insists the case is simple.
memories.memory_text: Cam suggested we review the inventory list, but I told him this was a simple case—thieves came through the roof and stole stuff—so there was no need to delay closing it.

grounded_facts: Cam questions why a valuable computer was left behind during the supposed burglary.
Cam raises a doubt about why valuable items like the computer were left behind.
memories.memory_text: I was in the office when Cam asked me why the thieves would leave behind a nice computer, questioning why such a valuable item wasn't taken during the supposed burglary.

grounded_facts: Tiffany stops Ted from repeatedly watching the body footage by taking the remote control, marking a turning point in her tolerance of his obsession.
Tiffany physically removes the remote control from Ted to stop his repetitive viewing of the body footage.
memories.memory_text: I was rewinding and replaying the body footage again when Tiffany walked over and took the remote from me, stopping me.

grounded_facts: A focused, informal session in which Ted reviews video evidence and case files related to the ongoing investigation, joined by Tiffany.
memories.memory_text: I was reviewing the body footage and case files on the wall, trying to piece together what happened, with Tiffany in the room.

grounded_facts: Tiffany tells Ted to re-examine the case file, specifically pointing to new information about the victim's record.
memories.memory_text: I was told by Tiffany to re-examine the case file, specifically to look at new information about the victim's record.

grounded_facts: Tiffany urges Ted to re-examine the case file, prompting a potential shift in investigative focus.
memories.memory_text: I saw Tiffany scan the file and then she tossed it to me after saying I should read it again, which made me reconsider where to focus my investigation.

grounded_facts: Ted directly accuses Paul of murder and declares his intent to see him jailed.
memories.memory_text: I confronted Paul and told him I would personally see to it that he went to jail for killing that man and dumping his body in the woods.

grounded_facts: Ted observes Paul's bruises after helping him up, showing curiosity about their origin.
memories.memory_text: I helped Paul up and noticed his bruises, so I asked him, 'Hey, how'd you get all cut up?'

grounded_facts: Mrs. Wherry intervenes with a weapon to defend Paul when Ted becomes threatening.
memories.memory_text: I saw Mrs. Wherry step in with a weapon and heard her tell me to move away from Paul, so I backed off.

grounded_facts: After Mrs. Wherry offers to intervene, Paul declines her help and insists on handling the confrontation with Ted himself, indicating a shift toward self-reliance or concealment.
memories.memory_text: I heard Paul tell Mrs. Wherry he was fine and then say to me that I'd better go, which made me think he wanted to handle things on his own.

grounded_facts: A tense encounter between Paul and Ted at Paul's mobile home, involving accusations of murder and physical confrontation, interrupted by Mrs. Wherry's armed intervention.
memories.memory_text: I remember the tension rising when I accused Paul—he got aggressive, stabbed his shovel into the snow, tried to push me away, slipped, and fell, and then Mrs. Wherry showed up with a gun, so I backed off to my car and left.

grounded_facts: After falling and reopening his forehead wound, Paul examines his blood and begins formulating a new plan or realization.
memories.memory_text: I saw Paul stab his shovel into the snow and walk over, then later I noticed him looking at blood on his fingers like he was figuring something out.

grounded_facts: Ted confronts Paul after hearing him speak to Branch, denying any violence and demanding to present evidence.
memories.memory_text: I confronted Paul directly, asking if he really thought I did this, and I told him, 'Oh come on. I never laid a hand on him.'

grounded_facts: Paul meets with Branch in the insurance office, accusing Ted of misconduct; Ted interrupts and presents counter-evidence about Raymond's body.
memories.memory_text: I walked into my boss' office and saw Paul talking to Branch, and when I came in, Paul mentioned that he was discussing our meeting, implying he had concerns about me.

grounded_facts: Ted shows Paul and Branch a video of the morgue body, the police file, and a photo of Raymond with a visible birthmark, arguing that the body lacks the documented birthmark and thus may not be Raymond's.
memories.memory_text: I showed Paul and Branch the video of the morgue body, the police file, and the photo of Raymond with the birthmark on his leg, pointing out that the body doesn't have the mark and asking them to see the difference.

grounded_facts: Paul claims Raymond had laser surgery in Florida to remove the birthmark, providing a plausible but likely false explanation for its absence on the morgue body.
memories.memory_text: I remember Paul telling me that Raymond had laser surgery in Florida to remove the birthmark, saying it was like getting a tattoo taken off.

grounded_facts: Paul seizes moral high ground by accusing Ted of taping his brother's naked body and stealing family photos, framing him as sick and invasive.
memories.memory_text: I was confronted by Paul, who accused me of taping his brother's naked body in the morgue and stealing family photos, calling me sick and invasive.

grounded_facts: Branch ends the meeting by agreeing to pay Paul compensation and orders Ted to deliver a formal apology, effectively siding with Paul despite doubts.
Branch shuts down Ted's argument, reprimands him for appearance of misconduct, and orders him to deliver an apology and check.
memories.memory_text: I remember arguing with Branch, trying to tell him Paul was in the wrong, but he shut me down and told me to deliver a check and a full apology to Paul the next day — I could tell he was more worried about covering our backs than about what actually happened.

grounded_facts: Branch reveals that Cam has found an 'out' on the warehouse robbery case, leading to a promotion and potential transfer, undermining Ted's position.
Branch informs Ted that Cam has been promoted for solving the warehouse case, diminishing Ted's value in the company.
memories.memory_text: I was told by Branch that Cam found an 'out' on the warehouse robbery case, and because of that, head office is promoting him—which undermines my position and makes me feel less valued.

grounded_facts: After being overruled and upstaged, Ted storms out of Branch's office, slamming the door.
memories.memory_text: I stormed out of Branch's office and slammed the door after being overruled and upstaged.

grounded_facts: Raymond physically dominates Ted and issues a direct verbal threat demanding compliance.
memories.memory_text: I was hit and then Raymond, wearing a ski mask, crushed my head against the car door while yelling at me to comply with his demands.

grounded_facts: Raymond, wearing a ski mask, violently attacks Ted by punching him and crushing his head against the car door jamb to threaten him.
memories.memory_text: I saw Raymond in a ski mask punch me, pick me up, and slam my head into the car door jamb before taking my wallet.

grounded_facts: After threatening Ted, Raymond takes his wallet from him before leaving.
memories.memory_text: I was walking to my car when suddenly I was punched in the face, and then Raymond, wearing a ski mask, slammed my head into the door jamb and crushed it as I screamed—I thought I was going to die—until he finally let go and took my wallet before walking away.

grounded_facts: Ted challenges Paul's claim of loving his wife, implying disbelief and suspicion about Paul's role in Raymond's death.
memories.memory_text: I challenged Paul's claim that he loved his wife, implying he didn't mean it, because I still suspect him in Raymond's death.

grounded_facts: While Paul is distracted, Ted sees the Sea Shell in the open drawer, leading to a moment of emotional and symbolic tension.
memories.memory_text: I saw the Sea Shell in Paul's drawer when he opened it, and later I picked it up and turned it over in my hands while he was distracted.

grounded_facts: Avis retrieves the Sea Shell from Ted and reattaches it to the Aloha Air promotional display, restoring its public position.
memories.memory_text: I had the shell in my hands, and then Avis came in, saw it, took it from me, and put it back on the Aloha Air display.

grounded_facts: The lights go out in the travel agency, plunging Ted, Paul, and Avis into darkness during the transaction.
memories.memory_text: I was standing there with Paul and Avis when the lights suddenly went out, and we were all plunged into darkness.

grounded_facts: After Paul signs, Ted hands over the check but refuses to release it immediately, creating a moment of physical and emotional tension.
memories.memory_text: I handed the check to Paul after he signed, but I didn't let go right away, and I could feel the tension as he tried to pull it from my hand.

grounded_facts: A formal meeting at the travel agency where Ted delivers and processes the check and documents with Paul.
Ted brings and hands over the check and documents to Paul for signing, marking a formal transaction between them.
memories.memory_text: I arrived at the travel agency with the check and documents, and when Paul came over, I told him, 'Mr. Barnell. I have your check.' I slid the papers to him and handed over the envelope, but I didn't let go right away—I kept my grip until he signed, making sure he felt the weight of it.

grounded_facts: After Ted leaves, Paul sits alone in the dark office, illuminated only by a flashlight, suggesting isolation or contemplation.
memories.memory_text: I left Paul alone in the dark office, and as I walked away, I realized he was sitting completely still, lit only by a small flashlight—maybe he finally had time to think about what he's done.

grounded_facts: Tiffany, posing as a psychic, advises Paul that love is sacrifice and encourages him to take action to protect his wife, framing the call as entertainment.
Tiffany reassures Paul that his feelings are valid and affirms his willingness to sacrifice for his wife.
Tiffany conducts a paid psychic consultation with Paul, who calls under distress about moral conflict regarding protecting his wife.
memories.memory_text: I was on the sofa, half-watching TV while Tiffany did one of her paid psychic calls, and I remember her telling Paul that love is sacrifice, reassuring him that his feelings were valid and encouraging him to protect his wife—all while framing it as entertainment.

grounded_facts: Ted snorts in response to Tiffany's use of a familiar phrase, signaling derision or irony.
Ted snorts in response to Tiffany's use of the phrase 'love is sacrifice,' indicating skepticism or irony toward her performance.
memories.memory_text: I snorted when Tiffany used that familiar phrase, 'love is sacrifice,' because it came off as so clichéd and insincere in that moment.

grounded_facts: Ted and Cam are at Nick's strip bar during the night, engaging in conversation over drinks.
memories.memory_text: I was sitting at the bar beside Cam that night, just trying to drink in peace.

memories.memory_text: Cam told me he owed me thanks for giving him a shot on a case, and then he asked about what happened to my face, like we were close or something.

grounded_facts: Ted responds to Cam's gratitude and personal question with sarcasm and minimal engagement, ultimately ending the interaction by leaving.
memories.memory_text: I gave him a sarcastic reply and shut down the conversation because I didn't want to talk about it, then got up to leave.

grounded_facts: Ted, after a brief conversation with Cam, stands up and exits the bar despite being unsteady on his feet.

memories.memory_text: I tried to close the fridge door, but it wouldn't shut all the way—something was blocking it from the inside. I hip-checked it hard and heard a crack, like ice splitting in a freezer tray.
I heard Paul say Raymond was back, and something in my chest just locked—next thing I knew, I was rushing out of that kitchen.
I was pushing the vacuum and humming, feeling like I was getting something done, when suddenly it roared to life without me doing anything—didn’t even flinch, just kept going.

I asked Paul if Raymond was here—if he was anywhere near us—and for a second, just saying it out loud made my chest tighten. Then Paul said he’d probably be gone soon, and I could finally breathe again.
I called out to Paul, asking who was out there, but he didn’t answer me—just blocked the door from opening like I wasn’t even there.

I stood in the doorway, shaky, and told Paul I’d taken Adavan and called my psychic—then I showed him the HMO letter. When he started reading it, I just broke down, sobbing because I knew what it said before he even finished.

I screamed that I was really sick, over and over, my voice cracking—I could feel the panic rising, like if I didn’t make him see how bad it was, no one ever would. I was terrified he’d think I was just crazy, not dying.
I kept grinning at everyone, even though I didn’t feel like it—just kept my teeth showing, probably looked crazy, but I couldn’t stop.
I saw Gary messing with the fridge—our fridge—and when I saw that dead man’s hair hanging inside, I didn’t hesitate. I started hurling everything I could grab at him, cans, tools, whatever was there.
I grabbed the portable phone and started dialing, telling him he was in deep trouble—then I threw it right at his head when he raised the gun.
I'm sitting at our kitchen table with tape over my mouth, unable to speak, watching Paul freeze when he sees me like this.
I told Gary my cursing wasn't just attitude—it was Tourette's, a real disease—and right after, I couldn't stop myself from blurting out 'ass-rimming ball-sucker' even though he was holding a gun.

When he picked up the gun and tried to scare me into silence, I stared him down and told him to put it down or I'd scream so loud he'd have to shoot me—felt the tape biting into my wrists the whole time.
I told Jimbo Gary was just tired, like it was no big deal, even though I could feel his fingers on my wrist like he was checking a corpse.
I shouted into the bathroom that I had a psychiatric disorder—and that he did too—like throwing a knife and watching it stick.
I said it tasted like a rectal polyp—watched Gary’s face fall and Jimbo’s eyes dart to me, then back at his plate like he couldn’t believe I’d actually said it out loud.

I scooched across the bed with my hands tied to my chest, used the phone by pressing it flat against the mattress, and managed to dial 911—but when I heard the recording, I just shut it off with my nose.
I finally got through to someone, and when I told him there was a man with a gun in my shower, he actually recognized my name—called me 'Mrs. Barnell' like he could see me, like he knew who I was.
I'm still sitting right by the phone, stuck in this damn spot, while Gary sings that stupid show tune from the shower—can't think straight with him yowling like that.
I told them the gay mafia was coming to kill me in the park, and I could hear Ted struggling to speak in the background, all choked up and desperate like he actually believed me.
I heard the shower shut off—shit, he was done—so I slammed the phone down, shoved the gag back in, and scrambled to get back in position before he walked out.
I made up that emergency call, gave Ted the fake address, and waited to see if he’d actually leave Tiffany for it—felt a cold rush when the phone kept ringing and I knew he was walking out the door.
I was dragged into the garage with my hands tied, and I saw Jimbo pick up Jodie like it was nothing, just shoving him back inside while I couldn't do a damn thing.

Gary shoved a magazine in my face, pointing at some symptom list like he was playing armchair doctor, and said I was faking Tourette's. I told him magazines don't prove anything, not with that smug look he had.

I laughed through the gag in the backseat, sharp and sudden, watching Jimbo and Gary stiffen up like I’d kicked the seat. They didn’t look back, didn’t say a word—just drove on like I wasn’t even there.
I smiled and whispered to Paul, asking if food poisoning counted as being hurt—he looked bruised, so I touched his face and asked if he fell.
Paul quietly told me to walk to that hill and keep going no matter what, then slipped his red parka over my shoulders—said if he didn't catch up, I should look inside it.
I felt a hard impact in my back, like someone kicked me, and then I couldn't breathe—everything went heavy and dark as I collapsed into the snow.
I felt Paul turning me over, and when I could finally gasp for air, I realized I wasn't bleeding—I was alive, the bullet must've hit the money stack in my back.
I stood in the living room, watching Paul read my postcard, then asked him if he was ready—seeing him look up at me, finally really seeing me there, after everything.
I picked up Jodie’s carrier, felt Paul squeeze my hand, and heard the cab honk outside—then said I was feeling pretty damn good, and meant it.

memories.memory_text: I was on the phone with the electric company, trying to explain I pay my bills, when I saw those repo men approaching my office—distracted for just a second, and the phone slipped right out of my grip into the dumpster.
I reached in to grab the phone, pushed aside a wet garbage bag, and then saw him—a man in a cheap suit, skin a little blue, with my phone resting across his mouth like he was still talking.
I had to kick the knee to make the body fit—felt it snap sideways, cold and wrong under my foot. I looked away, breathing hard, trying not to throw up.

After locking the fridge with the chain and padlock, I kicked the stray cans into the corner and walked inside, asking about mail like nothing happened—voice steady, but my hands wouldn’t stop trembling.
I told Margaret over dinner that Raymond was back—just came out with it while shutting the oven door. I smiled like it was nothing, but she didn’t buy it, not for a second.
I was watching the home video of Raymond at the VFW party when he threw me down. Later, I found his birth certificate while going through the box.

I flipped through the newspaper, section by section, looking for any sign that someone had reported a missing person—nothing. Then I stood there, hand resting on the cold fridge door, talking to the body inside like it could hear me, wondering if anyone was left who’d care enough to want him buried properly.

I held up the seashell from my office and let the tears come—just enough—saying it was all we had left of him, that he’d been gone five years. When Boyle asked if it was my brother, I looked at that ruined face and nodded, saying they chewed his ears off.

I stood on the stoop under the camera light, squinting, trying to sound steady—'Obviously, my wife's very upset'—while my hand stayed tight on the door handle behind me, holding it shut as Margaret hammered from the other side.

I heard her scream 'Who fucked with the fucking door!' and felt the jolt in the handle—my fingers stayed locked on it, even as I said we had to plan a service, then finally let go and stepped inside, shutting her noise out for a second.
I remember sitting at my desk, the silence pressing in, and feeling my chest tighten when Ted asked about how often Raymond hiked—like he was digging for something I wasn’t ready to give up.
I remember holding that HMO letter, trying to read it through Margaret’s sobs—her hands shaking, the paper crumpling a little in my grip. I said 'Shush, now,' like that would fix anything.

I asked if maybe it wasn’t Tourette’s—just stress—remembering how she was on that cruise, calm, smiling. The second I said it, I saw her face fall, and I regretted it, but I was tired, so tired of not knowing what was real.
I checked my watch and glanced at Margaret—she was smiling at everyone again, like nothing was wrong, while the snow finally let up.

I called the news crews myself—let them trudge through the snow just in time for the burial. When Ted saw them, I could tell he was caught off guard, so I offered to walk down together, suggested he might want to tell them the check is on its way.

I walked in, just like any other day, called out to Maggie—then froze. She was sitting there with tape over her mouth, Gary and that other man flanking her, and I nearly charged them before seeing the gun.
Jimbo mentioned the dead man behind my office, and I tried to play dumb—but then Gary threw that frozen clump of hair on the table. I knew right then. They had the evidence. I was done.
I remember standing in the living room, pacing, when Gary figured it out—just like that. He looked at me and said, 'So what'd you collect?' and I knew there was no lying my way out.
He said if I didn’t bring the body and $50,000, they’d start mailing my wife back in pieces—starting with her feet. I remember the pause, the way he said it, like it was just business.

I stepped out of the car with just a K-Mart bag, my face still wet from crying, and Mrs. Wherry called out her condolences about Raymond—I managed a sad smile, said I was only staying a bit, then went inside without looking back.

I opened the door, and a gloved hand slammed it into me—I crashed into the wall, the family picture shattered on my head, and then Raymond picked me up and threw me through the serving hatch. I couldn’t breathe, just saw him standing there like nothing had changed.

He sat beside me on the floor, lit a cigarette, and asked about the life insurance—'So where's my money?' I could barely catch my breath, but I told him they were still investigating. When he shrugged and said fifty thousand was almost worth coming back for, I agreed to split it, just to keep him calm.
Raymond stood too close, talking about visiting the debtor himself, and I rushed to pull the blinds shut—someone might’ve seen him, and that would’ve ruined everything.

I dropped to my knees, dizzy and retching, one hand on my chest like I could hold myself together—tears came before I could stop them, and I just kept whispering to Mag Pie to hang on, like that would fix anything.

I walked in and saw him—drunk, loud, with those women hanging off him—acting like we weren’t hiding, like we weren’t supposed to be invisible. I barely got out, 'Could... I have a word with you?' before my throat tightened up.

I saw the gun on the counter after Raymond pulled out the credit card—my name was on that card, and now there's a damn handgun just sitting there like it belongs. I poked it, and the barrel spun right toward me.

My phone rang, and Jimbo was on the other end asking if I was having a party—then Gary started counting down, demanding to know if I had the body, and Margaret screamed through the gag about being threatened in the kitchen.

I was sitting in the dark with the phone bill in front of me, asking if it was okay to do something really bad to stop someone else from doing something worse—I don’t even know if he meant it, but I couldn’t shake the feeling he might.
I walked in and slammed the door hard behind me, then said it plain—'She's having sex with them'—before heading straight back to the bedroom without looking to see how Raymond took it.

I told Ray about seeing Margaret in the bedroom with that big guy, and how it wasn't the first time—other men, not kidnappers. My voice dropped when I said it, like I was afraid someone else might hear, even though it was just us.
Ray compared her to Mom's sick dog, saying the only way to stop the mess was to put it out of its misery. I asked if he was sure, and when he said yes, I nodded—even though my chest felt torn open.
I asked Avis to call me Paul—just Paul—because the formality felt pointless now, with no customers and everything falling apart.
I stood in the back room, surrounded by floating down feathers from my torn parka, and told Avis to get my passport, tape, and two open-ended tickets to Paraguay—my voice tight, almost frayed.
I had the gun pointed right at his forehead, my finger on the trigger... but then I really looked at him—just this drooling, sleeping man, almost peaceful. I couldn't do it.
I emptied the bullets into a glass of water and hid it on the top shelf—cold, quiet, like burying something without a grave. Then I put the gun back, useless.
I opened the trunk and stood back as Jimbo and Gary looked inside. Gary reached down and touched the body, asking how they knew it was Raymond.
After they looked at the body, I handed the ransom money to Gary. I don’t know if they believed me, but the exchange happened.

memories.memory_text: I offered to help Howard unload his snowmobile, handed him the two-by-eights to make a ramp, and when his back was turned, I took out the camcorder and started recording.
Howard turned around, saw the camera, and confronted me—I didn’t lower it, just kept filming as he asked what I thought I was doing.

I played the recording of Howard, and the coworkers actually clapped—just a little wave over the cubicle was enough. Then I muttered to myself, 'After all they've done for me,' because the irony wasn't lost on me, not one bit.

I was driving home, flipping through radio stations, not liking any of them. I landed on 'Escape (The Piña Colada Song)' when I saw a moose in the road. I slammed the brakes and stopped about five feet away. The moose looked at me, then walked off.

I came home and saw Tiffany in my apartment, feet up on the desk, wearing a headset connected to my computer. A zodiac screensaver was on the screen. She was flipping through a copy of 'Cosmo.' My place felt cluttered, like my space wasn't just mine anymore.

I was finally letting myself say it out loud—how much I've given to Liberty Capital and how I deserve more than this frozen nowhere job, but then the moment got cut off by the phone ringing, and Tiffany’s smile faded like she didn’t believe in it anymore.
I asked Boyle if it didn't strike him as suspicious that Barnell's brother had tried to cash the policy two weeks earlier, and he just brushed it off like it meant nothing.
I pulled out the camcorder and started filming the body myself when Boyle wouldn't let us investigate properly—he told me to stop, but I got the shots I needed before he slammed the drawer shut.
I remember pushing back when Branch shut down the investigation, saying it stinks and corporate wouldn't like us burying it—but he just said corporate's view would be whatever he told them.
I asked Paul if Raymond hiked often, pressing him on whether it was a regular thing or just something he did once—something didn’t add up and I needed to know what he was hiding.
I called in a favor to run credit checks on Raymond and Paul Barnell, staying on the line while the request processed, my voice low but firm at the desk.
I pulled Cam into my cubicle and made promises—more inclusion, better behavior—just to buy time, knowing we could get caught.

I had to cut her off—she was drifting into gossip about Paul’s wife, but I needed to know about Raymond. When I asked if he was an outdoorsman, she hesitated, then said he wasn’t, but mentioned cops used to come by the cabin all the time.

She said she thought it was Paul clearing her driveway at first—then dropped that line about the ski mask. 'You can hardly tell who's who.' That didn’t sit right. Could mean someone was misidentified, or worse—someone was covering their face.

I remember chewing jerky at my desk, snow blowing outside, and realizing Raymond Barnell had no credit history for five years—nothing. Then I saw he’d only recently gotten new ID and a credit card with no charges. It didn’t make sense, but I knew it was something.

I was standing at the gravesite, watching Paul walk away after he told me he called the media himself—then I saw a photo of his brother blow into the snow at my feet and picked it up without thinking.

I looked up through the hole in the roof and approved the $200,000 claim on the spot—Cam wanted to check the inventory first, but this was straightforward: thieves came through the roof, took the goods, case clear.

I was replaying the footage, frame by frame—had to see it again, had to catch what I missed. When she grabbed the remote, all I could think was she didn’t understand how close I was to seeing it clearly.

She said she was trying to be supportive, and I fumbled the words—almost said 'complaints about my wife' but stopped myself. Tossed out 'you' instead. Felt the weight of what I almost admitted, then she threw the file back at me like it meant something.
I told Paul straight up he was going to jail—I said I’d personally see to it—after calling him out for murder and lying about Raymond.
When Paul slipped and fell in the snow, I grabbed him to help up and saw the bruises on his face—looked like he’d been in a bad fight.

I pulled the video, the police file, and that photo from my briefcase and showed them exactly where the birthmark was missing—right there on the screen, clear as day. I could see the doubt hit Paul when I pointed it out.

I had the moment—finally—after laying it all out, pacing while the tape played, feeling like I’d turned the whole thing around. Then it just… stopped. No acknowledgment, no shift in their stance, just silence hanging there.
I opened my car door and then a fist slammed into my face—I was on the ground before I could react, my head crushed against the door frame, screaming as he pressed down.
After he let go, I was still on the ground, dazed—I didn't resist when he leaned down and took my wallet, just watched him walk away.

I handed Paul the check and watched his face when he saw my bruises—he knew where they came from, even if he didn’t say it. I called it a mugging, but the way he froze told me he understood it wasn’t random.

I moved behind his shoulder as he sat at the desk, watching him sign—close enough to see if he flinched, if he gave anything away. When I saw that shell on his desk, I couldn’t look away; it felt like it didn’t belong, like it was left there on purpose.
I snorted when Tiffany said 'love is sacrifice'—it came out before I could stop it, and then she just glared at me, cold. I tried to catch her eye afterward, but she wouldn’t look back.

I remember stumbling through the snow, shoving that 'For Sale' sign over with my hands — it toppled into the white like it meant nothing. I tried to light it, but the matches wouldn't catch, and then I just felt the cold, sharp and real, pulling me back to the car.
I saw Margaret Barnell’s name on the screen—her file open with notes about her delusions—and realized she was talking about a man with a gun in her shower like it was real.
I reached for the headset when Tiffany walked in, trying to get it back so I could respond—she didn’t understand, but I needed to say something.

I was pulling on my boots, ready to go, and she said maybe we shouldn’t be together like this—just stood there watching me, not picking up the phone, not stopping me. I had nothing to say, so I left, slammed the door behind me.

I came back in, told her she needed to come with me—not sarcastic, not joking—and when she asked why, I said if she didn’t, I’d have to stay, and that would ruin everything. She smiled, actually believed me.
I smiled and started talking—actually talking—about things I’ve never said out loud, just let it go while she listened.
I took the turnoff to the parking area after saying we’d arrived—no more speculation, time to see what Barnell was really up to.
I confronted Raymond, asked if he was who I thought he was, and immediately realized how bad that sounded—especially when he looked at me like I was a threat.
After he elbowed me in the temple, I went down hard—but I still reached out and grabbed his ankle before he could walk away.
